stories.headline: AI BUBBLE FEARS TRIGGER NASDAQ-100'S WORST SESSION SINCE JUNE
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 sank 2.50% to 29,187.55 and the S&P 500 fell 1.09% to 7,659.44 as a global tech selloff, sparked by weakness in Korea's chip-heavy KOSPI, spread to Wall Street on renewed doubts about AI capital spending. The Nasdaq is now down more than 4% on the week, its worst since June.
stories.explain: Mega-cap tech names carry outsized weight in both indices, so any repricing of AI-related capex (debt-funded data center buildouts, chip orders) moves the whole market even when the news is sector-specific. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the hundreds of billions being spent on AI infrastructure will generate matching returns, and that doubt compresses the high multiples those stocks trade at. Because the Nasdaq 100 is cap-weighted, a handful of AI-exposed giants falling 4-5% can drag the whole index down 2%+ even when market breadth is only modestly negative.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 5.07% AS FLIGHT TO SAFETY OFFSETS HOT CPI
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.07%, well off the 5.3%+ spike hit just two days earlier after September's hotter-than-expected CPI print. The pullback came as investors rotated out of equities and into bonds during today's tech-led risk-off move.
stories.explain: Normally a hot CPI report pushes yields higher because it raises the odds the Fed holds rates higher for longer. But when a sharp equity selloff hits at the same time, a 'flight to quality' bid for Treasuries can dominate, pushing bond prices up and yields down even as the inflation backdrop argues for the opposite. That tug-of-war, inflation data pulling yields up while risk-off flows pull them down, is exactly what produced this week's round trip from above 5.3% to 5.07%.

stories.headline: WTI SURGES 3.4% TO $101 ON HORMUZ TENSIONS, STEEP INVENTORY DRAW
stories.body: WTI crude jumped $3.40, or 3.4%, to $101.34 a barrel (Brent near $109.44) after fresh tension around the Strait of Hormuz and an EIA report showing U.S. crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels in the week ended October 9, well above consensus.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil flows, so any perceived threat to shipping there adds a geopolitical risk premium independent of actual supply disruption. Layer on an inventory draw nearly double what traders expected, a signal of stronger demand or tighter domestic supply, and crude gets a two-sided catalyst: a risk premium plus a fundamentals surprise, which is why the move was so outsized relative to a typical session.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS AS TECH SELLOFF TRIGGERS CASH-RAISING, NOT A SAFE-HAVEN BID
stories.body: Spot gold eased about 0.4% to roughly $4,168 an ounce even as stocks sold off, a sign the metal is being used as a funding source rather than a hedge. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's refusal to rule out a rate hike also weighed on bullion.
stories.explain: Gold is supposed to rally when stocks fall, but that only holds when investors are rotating into havens rather than scrambling for cash. When a selloff is sharp enough to trigger margin calls, funds instead sell whatever is liquid, including gold, to raise cash and meet those calls, which can push gold down in the same session stocks are falling. A hawkish Fed signal compounds that by raising the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold relative to cash or Treasuries.

stories.headline: $2 TRILLION DEFICIT, 5% YIELDS SEEN AS NEXT BIG FISCAL CHALLENGE
stories.body: Strategists are flagging the combination of a roughly $2 trillion annual federal deficit and Treasury yields sitting near 5% as a structural headwind, warning that debt-service costs are climbing even as the government must keep issuing more supply to cover the gap.
stories.explain: When yields rise, every dollar of maturing debt has to be refinanced at a higher rate, which mechanically increases the interest bill on outstanding debt with a lag. At a $2 trillion deficit, higher-for-longer yields don't just cost more directly, they also mean more new issuance is needed to fund that deficit, which itself puts upward pressure on yields by increasing bond supply, a dynamic some strategists worry can become self-reinforcing.

stories.headline: FLORIDA PROJECTED NO. 1 IN PRESEASON AP POLL FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2006
stories.body: With the official preseason AP Top 25 due out before next week's season openers, multiple outlets project Florida as the No. 1 team, with Duke and Illinois rounding out the top three. It would be Florida's first preseason No. 1 ranking since 2006.

stories.headline: NBA TIPS OFF 2026-27 SEASON TUESDAY; GIANNIS, LEBRON DEBUTS LOOM
stories.body: The new season opens Tuesday at 3 p.m. ET with Boston at Detroit, followed by Philadelphia-New York and Oklahoma City-San Antonio. Giannis Antetokounmpo debuts for Miami on Oct. 21 and LeBron James begins a record 24th season with the 76ers, while reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and three-time MVP Nikola Jokic headline the early award race.

stories.headline: TRADE DEADLINE BUZZ: RAVENS LAND JURGENS, CARDINALS MOVE ON FROM HARRISON JR.
stories.body: Baltimore acquired center Cam Jurgens from Philadelphia after losing multiple centers to injury, while Arizona parted ways with 2024's No. 4 overall pick, receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. Pittsburgh also dealt cornerback Porter to Dallas, ending a monthslong contract standoff.

stories.headline: GEORGIA RISES TO NO. 1 AFTER TEXAS LOSS; NOTRE DAME, MIAMI ROUND OUT TOP THREE
stories.body: Georgia moved to No. 1 in the latest AP Top 25 after once-top-ranked Texas fell to No. 7 following a loss, with Notre Dame at No. 2 and Miami at No. 3. Ohio State and Indiana round out the top five heading into this week's slate.

deepDive.title: Why Hot Inflation Can Still Send Yields Down: Flight-to-Quality vs. the Inflation Signal
content: Today's brief contains an apparent contradiction: September CPI ran hotter than expected, which should have pushed the 10-year Treasury yield higher as markets priced in a Fed that stays restrictive for longer. Instead, the 10-year sits near 5.07%, down sharply from the 5.3%-plus spike it hit just two trading days after that CPI print. The resolution is that two forces were pulling on yields at once, and today the second one won. Knowing which force dominates, and when, is one of the more practical skills in fixed income, because it determines whether a hot inflation print is actually a buy or sell signal for bonds on any given day.

The first force is the textbook one: hotter inflation data raises the expected path of the fed funds rate, and since longer-term yields are roughly the average of expected future short rates plus a term premium, higher expected short rates push the 10-year up. That is exactly what happened in the hours after the CPI release. The second force is flight-to-quality: when risk assets sell off hard, as the Nasdaq 100 did this week on AI-capex fears, large pools of capital rotate into Treasuries regardless of the inflation outlook, simply because Treasuries are the deepest, most liquid safe asset available. That buying pressure can overwhelm the inflation-driven move entirely.

What most people miss is that this isn't a coin flip: flight-to-quality tends to dominate over short, sharp equity drawdowns, while the inflation signal tends to reassert itself once the panic fades. The clearest precedent is March 2020, when CPI data was irrelevant for weeks as the 10-year collapsed toward 0.5% purely on equity-market panic, even though nothing about the inflation outlook had changed. A smaller version just played out here: yields spiked on the CPI release, then round-tripped lower as the tech rout took over. The size and speed of the equity move is usually the tell for which regime you're in.

For today's setup, that framework suggests the yield pullback is more about the AI selloff than about the Fed suddenly turning dovish, consistent with Fed Chair Warsh's refusal to rule out a rate hike even as yields fell. It also explains gold's odd decline alongside the stock rout: gold usually benefits from the same flight-to-quality bid helping Treasuries, but when a selloff is sharp enough to trigger margin calls, funds sell liquid assets, gold included, to raise cash, temporarily breaking its normal haven behavior. If next week's Q3 earnings calm the AI-capex worries, expect the inflation signal to reassert itself and yields to drift back toward that 5.3% level.
